title: How Vaccines Work
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: Every day the human body is attacked by bacteria and viruses, and most of the time we never notice, because the immune system defeats them. White blood cells find invaders by recognising antigens, which are molecules on the surface of a germ. When a new germ is met for the first time, the response is slow, and a person may be ill for days before the body wins. Without this defence, even a minor infection could be fatal, and for most of history, many of them were.

The key discovery was that the immune system has a memory. After an infection, some of the white blood cells survive as memory cells, which can recognise the same germ years later and react within hours. A second infection is therefore usually much milder than the first, or does not cause illness at all. A vaccine is a way of giving the immune system this memory without the illness, and it is one of the cheapest and most effective tools in the history of medicine.

The idea is older than the science. In 1796 the English doctor Edward Jenner noticed that milkmaids who had caught cowpox, a mild disease, did not catch smallpox. He tested his idea on a boy by injecting him with material from a cowpox sore, and later showed that the boy was protected. The word vaccine comes from vacca, the Latin for cow. In 1980, after a worldwide campaign, the World Health Organization announced that smallpox had been wiped out, the only human disease to be defeated in this way.

Vaccines work in different ways. Some contain a weakened form of the germ, which can still multiply but cannot cause serious illness. Others contain a killed germ, or only a harmless part of it, such as a protein from its surface. A newer type, the mRNA vaccine, carries instructions that tell the body's own cells to make one harmless protein, which the immune system then learns to recognise. In every case, the aim is to show the immune system an antigen without the danger of the real disease.

Vaccines protect not only the people who receive them. When enough people in a community are immune, the germ finds it hard to spread, and those who cannot be vaccinated, such as newborn babies, gain some protection too. This effect is called herd immunity. The level needed depends on how infectious the disease is. For a disease that spreads slowly, a smaller share is enough, but for measles, which is highly infectious, about ninety-five per cent of people must be immune.

Like any medicine, vaccines can have side effects, but these are usually mild, such as a sore arm or a slight fever. Serious reactions are extremely rare. Before a vaccine is approved, it is tested in several phases, starting with small groups and ending with tens of thousands of volunteers, and its safety continues to be monitored afterwards. Doctors also record every report of illness after vaccination, so that a rare problem can be noticed quickly and investigated. Despite this, some people distrust vaccines, and false stories spread online have led to falling vaccination rates in some countries, and to the return of measles outbreaks.

Researchers are now working on vaccines for diseases that have resisted every attempt, including malaria, which kills more than half a million people a year. In 2021 the World Health Organization recommended a malaria vaccine for children in Africa, a breakthrough after decades of research. Other teams are exploring vaccines against some kinds of cancer. Such work is slow and expensive, but the rewards are large, because a successful vaccine can protect millions of children for the cost of a few coins each. Many experts believe that the next decades will see the most important advances since Jenner.
